tldr: L3MVN leverages large language models to impart common-sense knowledge for visual target navigation, eliminating the need for extensive scene prior learning. The framework uses language-based semantic reasoning to select relevant frontiers from semantic maps for efficient exploration.
contributions: A framework that builds environment maps and selects long-term goals based on frontiers using large language model inference for efficient exploration
Two paradigms (zero-shot and feed-forward) for semantic reasoning about objects using language models
Real-world robot evaluation demonstrating applicability and discussion of simulation-to-reality gap
methods: The framework constructs a semantic map from RGB-D images and extracts frontiers using a cost-utility scoring approach. For each frontier, objects are detected and filtered using entropy-based selection (top 15 lowest-entropy objects). Two LLM paradigms are used: (i) zero-shot uses pre-trained RoBERTa-large to score query strings like 'A frontier area containing [objects], [target]' for each target category, selecting the frontier with highest probability; (ii) feed-forward embeds a single query string and passes it through a fine-tuned three-layer neural network head to predict target category distributions. Frontier selection combines LLM scores with cost-utility scores using a bound B=[0.15, 0.3]. Local navigation employs the Fast Marching Method (FMM) with module-based obstacle avoidance.
results: On Gibson dataset: L3MVN zero-shot achieved 0.761 success rate (SPL 0.377, DTG 1.101), feed-forward achieved 0.769 success rate (SPL 0.388, DTG 1.008), outperforming SemExp (0.652 SR) and PONI (0.736 SR). On HM3D dataset: zero-shot achieved 0.504 success rate (SPL 0.231, DTG 4.427), feed-forward achieved 0.542 success rate (SPL 0.255, DTG 3.934), surpassing SemExp (0.379 SR). The method was also validated in real-world experiments for finding objects like sofas.
limitations: The paper acknowledges significant room for improvement in language-based approaches compared to task-specific learning
There remains a gap between simulation and real-world performance that requires further investigation
The approach depends on semantic segmentation accuracy from the finetuned RedNet model
Frontier areas may contain uninformative or unrelated objects (e.g., sofa in toilet), though entropy filtering partially addresses this
